title: Fluent adding and subtracting within 100
keyIdea: Being fluent within 100 means choosing a quick, reliable way for the numbers in front of you. Split both numbers into tens and ones when no number is near a ten (46 + 37 = 70 + 13 = 83). Round and adjust when one number is 1 or 2 from a ten (68 + 29 = 68 + 30 − 1 = 97; 83 − 19 = 83 − 20 + 1 = 64). Count up when two numbers are close (91 − 87: 87 → 90 → 91 is 4). Then check with the inverse: 83 − 25 = 58 because 58 + 25 = 83.
familyTip: When you see two prices, ask 'What's the quickest way?' before anyone works it out. For £68 + £29, say 'add 30 and take 1 back'. For 'how much more is 91p than 87p?', count up together: 3 to 90, 1 more to 91. Then ask your child to check a take-away by adding back.

visual.caption: Check each answer by adding back. Drag it, or tap it and then a box.

bins: adds back to the start: right
does not add back: a slip

lab.caption: Flagship lab: split into tens and ones, round and adjust, count up a small gap, pick the quickest strategy, check with the inverse.

kid: Look at the numbers first, then pick a quick way. One way is to split into tens and ones. For 46 + 37, add the tens: 40 + 30 = 70. Add the ones: 6 + 7 = 13. Then 70 + 13 = 83. The 13 has one more ten in it.
Round and adjust. 29 is one less than 30. So 68 + 29 is 68 + 30, take 1 away. That is 97. For 83 − 19, take away 20, then give 1 back. That is 64.
Count up when the numbers are close. For 91 − 87, go from 87 up to 90. That is 3. Then 1 more to 91. So the gap is 4.
Check by adding back. If 83 − 25 = 58, then 58 + 25 must make 83. It does, so the answer is right.
adult: Ages 7 to 8. This is CCSS 2.NBT.5 (fluently add and subtract within 100 using strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and the relationship between addition and subtraction) and the NC Year 2 and Year 3 mental calculation statements. Key words: partition, tens and ones, compensation (round and adjust), difference, counting up (complementary addition), inverse.

Fluency here is flexibility plus accuracy, not speed alone. Partitioning works for any pair and leans on place value. Compensation uses a near multiple of ten and then corrects the over- or under-shoot. Counting up treats subtraction as finding the difference, which is fastest when the two numbers are close. The inverse check turns every take-away into an addition the child already trusts.

Common mistakes: losing the extra ten when the ones total more than 9 (46 + 37 = 73); writing the parts side by side (713); adjusting the wrong way after rounding (68 + 29 = 99, or 83 − 19 = 62); taking the smaller ones digit from the larger regardless of order (83 − 25 = 62, since 5 − 3 = 2); and using one slow method, such as counting back in ones, for every question.

In the lab your child drags 40, 6, 30 and 7 into tens and ones boxes, taps a jump of 30 or 20 on a number line and then fixes it by 1, drags a dot to count up from 87 to 91, sorts six sums by the quickest strategy, and checks Sam's 83 − 25 = 62 by adding 62 + 25 = 87, then drags the answer to 58.

practice.prompt: What is the quickest way to work out 57 + 39?
practice.hint: Is 39 close to a whole ten? How far from 40 is it?
practice.explain: 39 is 1 less than 40. 57 + 40 = 97, then take back the extra 1: 96.

practice.hint: Add the tens, add the ones, then join them. Watch for an extra ten in the ones.
practice.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b}. Tens: {=a-a%10} + {=b-b%10}. Ones: {=a%10} + {=b%10}. Then add the two totals.

practice.prompt: Work out {a} − {=10*t-1} by taking away {=10*t} and then adjusting.
practice.hint: Take away {=10*t}. You took 1 too many, so give 1 back.
How far from {b} up to the next ten? Then how far from there to {=b+d}?

practice.prompt: Sam says 83 − 25 = 62. Which check shows the slip?
practice.hint: Adding undoes taking away. Add the answer to the number taken away.
practice.explain: 62 + 25 = 87, which is not 83, so 62 is wrong. Sam did 5 − 3. The right answer is 58, because 58 + 25 = 83.

pool.prompt: A shop has {a} red pens and {b} blue pens. How many pens is that?
pool.hint: Split both numbers into tens and ones. Do the ones make another ten?
pool.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b}. The ones {=a%10} + {=b%10} made more than 9, so one more ten joins the tens.

pool.hint: {=10*t-1} is 1 less than {=10*t}. Add {=10*t}, then take 1 away.

pool.prompt: Mo works out 68 + 29 as 68 + 30 + 1 = 99. What is the slip?
choices: 30 is 1 too many, so take 1 away: 97
pool.hint: Is 30 more or less than 29? Which way should the fix go?
pool.explain: 30 is 1 more than 29, so adding 30 adds 1 too many. Take it back: 98 − 1 = 97.

pool.prompt: Which is the quickest way to work out 73 − 68?
choices: split 68 into 60 and 8 and take each away
pool.explain: 68 to 70 is 2, 70 to 73 is 3, so the gap is 5. Counting back 68 ones would be very slow.

choices: Ali did 7 − 4 in the ones instead of taking a ten
pool.explain: 33 + 27 = 60, not 54. You cannot take 7 from 4, so take a ten: 14 − 7 = 7 and 4 tens − 2 tens = 2 tens. 54 − 27 = 27.

pool.hint: Add the answer to the number that was taken away.
pool.explain: 45 + 46 = 91, which is where we started, so 91 − 46 = 45 is right.

pool.hint: Can you take {=b%10} from {=a%10}? If not, take a ten first. Check by adding back.

pool.prompt: 46 + 37: why is the answer in the 80s, not the 70s?
pool.hint: Add the ones on their own. Is the total more than 9?
